nameStory: The name "spearwort" comes from the plant's narrow, spear-shaped leaves that look quite different from its round-leaved buttercup cousins. "Lesser" distinguishes it from other larger spearworts, though this little plant packs just as much beauty into its smaller frame. The old name "banewort" hints at its poisonous nature – "bane" meaning something harmful or destructive.
description: Lesser spearwort is a low-growing perennial wildflower that belongs to the buttercup family, but looks quite different from the typical buttercups you might know. Instead of the familiar lobed leaves, this plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that give it its spear-like appearance. It produces small, bright yellow flowers with five glossy petals and grows close to the ground, rarely getting taller than a foot. You'll find it creeping along wet areas where its stems can root at the nodes, forming small colonies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth and somewhat thick, completely unlike the deeply-lobed leaves of most buttercups – they really do look like little green spear points

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, bright yellow flowers with five shiny petals that gleam like they've been polished, much smaller than meadow buttercup blooms

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, creeping stems that often root where they touch the ground, creating a mat-like appearance rather than standing upright

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found in wet or boggy areas – if the ground isn't at least damp, you're probably looking at a different buttercup

habitat: Lesser spearwort thrives in consistently wet areas like pond edges, marshes, wet meadows, and boggy spots throughout New England. It prefers muddy or peaty soils that stay moist year-round and can tolerate having its roots in shallow standing water. You'll often find it growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other water-loving plants in these soggy habitats.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge early, with the distinctive narrow leaves appearing as soon as the ground thaws in wet areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period in June and July, when the small yellow flowers are most visible among the spear-shaped foliage.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back but may retain some green leaves if the weather stays mild and wet conditions persist.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the roots, leaving little trace above ground except in the mildest protected wetland areas.

funFact: This little buttercup has evolved a unique backup pollination system – when there aren't enough insects around, raindrops can actually pollinate the flowers by splashing pollen from the stamens onto the pistils, making it one of nature's rain-powered reproduction specialists!
confusionNotes: The narrow, unlobed leaves immediately separate lesser spearwort from all other buttercups except its close relative, creeping spearwort. Creeping spearwort has even more slender stems, narrower leaves, and smaller flowers – think of lesser spearwort as the "beefier" cousin.
contextualKnowledge: Like all members of the buttercup family, lesser spearwort is poisonous to both humans and livestock, containing compounds that can cause skin irritation and digestive problems if consumed. The old common name "banewort" was a warning about this toxic nature.
compareHints: Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves. Its closest relative, creeping spearwort, is even more delicate with thinner stems and tinier flowers, while lesser spearwort has a more robust appearance overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
